Read together, the four traditions converge on a single characterisation of ONC. Corpus-informed and corpus-supported Appraisal studies show that evaluation is a particularly salient characteristic of the register, central to what commenting is for, and that commenters prefer apparently objective Judgement and Appreciation over emotive Affect [@CavassoTaboada2021; @TrnavacTaboada2023]. Stancetaking research explains why: a comment is a public act of evaluating a shared object that positions its author and solicits alignment from others, an intersubjective logic that transfers directly to asynchronous written CMC [@DuBois2007; @GiaxoglouJohansson2020]. Corpus-driven work adds that such evaluative positioning is phraseologically patterned and community-specific: evaluative meaning resides in recurrent word sequences [@Hunston2011], and adjective-centred evaluative taxonomies differ between commenting communities [@MillarHunston2015; @Barbieri2018]. Even corpus-induced sentiment research, for all its loss of delicacy, presupposes that evaluation permeates the register. What none of these traditions has provided is a register-specific inventory of the recurrent lexico-grammatical formulae through which stance is taken in ONC. These findings converge on the present study's central construct through a chain of four steps. First, ONC are evaluative: evaluation is central to the communicative function of commenting. Second, evalution is realised linguistically through the resources of stance, the linguistic marking of attitudes, judgements and commitment [@BiberFinegan1988; @GrayBiber2012]. Third, at least some of these stance resources take the form of recurrent phraseological patterns rather than isolated items [@Biber2006; @Hunston2011]. Fourth, such patterns can be extracted automatically and inventoried for a register. Stance-related phraseological patterns therefore operationalise one important linguistic realisation of ONC's evaluative character: they are recurrent sequences defined over tagged stance features, such as evaluative adjectives, stance adverbs, private and suasive verbs, and modal verbs, whose attested lexical realisations are the bundles analysed in later chapters. The choice of these feature categories is motivated by the grammatical-stance framework of @BiberEtAl1999, which establishes them as core grammatical categories of stance marking: adjectives are the primary evaluative word class [@MillarHunston2015], adverbs function as stance adverbials, private and suasive verbs control stance complement clauses, and modal verbs mark epistemic and deontic stance. Complement-clause constructions and stance adverbials thus supply the grammatical framework within which the features are interpreted, while the patterns themselves are assembled from the tagged adjectives, adverbs, verbs and modals. The method therefore inherits the grammatical-stance grounding of the *Longman Grammar* framework [@BiberEtAl1999], while remaining extractable through automatic tagging. Chapter 4 develops this operationalisation for the ONC corpora of this study.

# Conclusion: toward the present study

## The argument of the chapter

Taken together, the literature reviewed in this chapter establishes three propositions about online news comments (ONC). The first is situational: ONC constitute a coherent discoursal configuration within computer-mediated communication (CMC), namely asynchronous, persistent, pseudonymous, one-to-many messages appended to professionally produced news texts [@Herring2007], functionally descended from the letter to the editor, but reconfigured by that migration into something more personal, more dialogic and less gatekept [@LandertJucker2011]. The second concerns register: read through the genre-versus-register distinction of Section 2 and the corpus typology of Section 3 [@BiberConrad2009; @Lee2008], comments are an emerging written register rather than the typed conversation early CMC research expected, patterning closest to opinion journalism and other persuasive written registers [@EhretTaboada2020; @EhretTaboada2021; cf. @Marchand2013; @Gerhardt2021], while at the genre level they participate in the larger hybrid unit of the participatory news article [@Bruce2010]. The third proposition is functional: evaluation is a particularly salient characteristic of the register, central to what commenting is for. Evaluative language saturates comments, skews strongly negative, and prefers apparently objective Judgement and Appreciation over emotive Affect [@CavassoTaboada2021], and stancetaking theory explains why: a comment is a public act of evaluating a shared object that simultaneously positions its author and solicits alignment from co-commenters [@DuBois2007]. In short, the field informs us what ONC are, where they sit among registers, and that evaluation is their main concern.

## What the literature cannot explain: the double gap

What this body of work cannot explain is how stance is performed, phraseologically, in the register. Each of Lee's [-@Lee2008] four approaches stops short of a register-specific phraseological inventory: corpus-informed genre analysis works at the level of whole texts [@Bruce2010]; corpus-supported annotation quantifies evaluative meanings rather than their recurrent wording [@KolhatkarEtAl2020; @CavassoTaboada2021]; corpus-induced sentiment methods achieve scale at the cost of linguistic interpretability; and even the corpus-driven tradition, which has shown stance to be phraseologically patterned and community-specific in adjacent comment data [@Barbieri2018; @MillarHunston2015], has produced no such inventory for news comments, the closest precedent being the exploratory bundle counts of @Marchand2013. The first gap, then, would appear to be that the field lacks a register-specific inventory of the recurrent lexico-grammatical formulae of stance in ONC. The second gap can also be stated provisionally for now: the literature reviewed here has not provided an account of how language learners deploy the register's characteristic stance resources; whether and to what extent learner corpus research has addressed the corresponding learner dimension will be taken up in Chapter 3. The double gap matters because register claims are only as strong as their comparisons: register features become visible only through contrast, and the evidentiary value of any corpus claim depends on demonstrable representativeness [@BiberConrad2009; @EgbertBiberGray2022]. I therefore use an early-2000s BBC *Have Your Say* corpus as a register benchmark rather than a strictly matched comparison corpus: it captures the first generation of moderated, public-service, below-the-line commenting [@Harrison2010; @Herring2004b], so that learner comments written more than a decade later can be located against an established native-speaker comment register with genre held broadly constant [@HerringPaolillo2006], and I treat the residual differences of writer population and period between the corpora as objects of interpretation rather than explaining them away.

## The design of the present study

The design developed in Chapter 4 follows directly from this argument, combining the two traditions best placed to close the first gap. Register description proceeds by additive multi-dimensional analysis, scoring the learner and reference comments on Biber's [-@Biber1988] dimensions: the additive variant is economical and yields scores directly comparable with the base study, the property that @Gerhardt2021 made use of for blog comments, while its known risk of dimensional misfit is mitigated by the convergence of Ehret and Taboada's [-@EhretTaboada2021] full MDA results on the written, argumentative-evaluative profile. Stance analysis proceeds through stance-related phraseological patterns: recurrent sequences defined over tagged stance features, such as evaluative adjectives, stance adverbs, private and suasive verbs, and modal verbs, together with their lexical realisations as bundles. As Section 5.6 detailed, these are core grammatical categories of stance marking established by @BiberEtAl1999: adjectives are the primary evaluative word class [@MillarHunston2015], adverbs function as stance adverbials, private and suasive verbs control stance complement clauses, and modal verbs mark epistemic and deontic stance; the stance-adverbial and complement-clause framework supplies the grammatical grounding [@Biber2006], comment-style data confirm these categories as the locus of evaluative meaning [@Barbieri2018], and the method remains extractable through automatic tagging. This second strand deliberately bridges the corpus-driven and corpus-supported approaches: extraction is inductive and automatic, but the patterns are classified against established functional categories and interpreted in co-text, retaining the interpretability that purely induced measures sacrifice. Chapter 3 first takes up the provisional learner gap through a second literature review, of learner corpus research (LCR), situating the L2 English writing of Japanese learners in particular. Chapter 4 then turns to the data itself, and to the construction of the corpora, the tagging procedure and the modelling strategy.
